title: Do I Need Bunion Surgery? When to Operate, and When Not To
metaDescription: A painful bump at the base of the big toe: which bunions need surgery, what helps without it, what the evidence says, and what recovery realistically involves.
intro: A bunion is a bony bump at the base of the big toe, where the toe has drifted towards the others. People often assume that because it will not straighten by itself, it must be operated on. That is not the case. Whether surgery makes sense depends on pain and function, not on how the foot looks.

sections.heading: Do all bunions need surgery?
sections.body: No. Surgery is only worth considering when a bunion stays painful, makes walking or footwear difficult despite sensible non-surgical measures, or is causing problems such as skin breakdown or crowding of the second toe. A bunion that looks prominent but does not bother you is not, on its own, a reason to operate. The deformity is progressive in many people, so it is worth having it checked, but progression is usually slow and a check-up is not the same as a decision to operate. What matters is how the foot works and feels, not how it looks in a photograph or on an X-ray.

sections.heading: What can I do without surgery, and what won't work?
sections.body: Wider shoes, soft padding, toe spacers, and sometimes orthotics or a night splint can reduce pain, and anti-inflammatory tablets can settle flare-ups. None of these reverses an established bunion, though they can ease symptoms and may slow progression. Be wary of gadgets that claim to realign the bone: there is no solid evidence for them. Footwear matters, since narrow pointed toe boxes push the toes into position, but family history also plays a large part, so a bunion is not simply the result of what you wear.
bullets: Wider shoes with a roomy toe box, and a flexible sole
Gel or silicone padding over the bump, tried briefly first (a badly fitted pad can add pressure)
Toe spacers or orthotics if they make walking more comfortable
Short courses of anti-inflammatory medication for flare-ups, if you can safely take them

sections.heading: When is surgery genuinely the right call?
sections.body: Surgery is reasonable when pain is disabling, when shoes and walking remain a problem after non-surgical treatment has had a fair trial, when a skin ulcer forms over the bump, or when the big toe is pushing the second toe out of joint. The aim is pain relief and better function. Surgery for appearance alone is not what the major patient-information sources recommend. If you have diabetes or reduced sensation in your feet, any open sore, redness or swelling around a bunion should be seen promptly rather than watched, because small problems in such feet can worsen quickly.

sections.heading: What does the evidence actually say about bunion surgery?
sections.body: The evidence is encouraging but thin. A 2024 Cochrane review of 25 studies found only one trial, of 140 people, comparing surgery with no treatment or non-surgical care. At 12 months pain was lower after surgery (21 versus 39 on a 0 to 100 scale) and satisfaction was higher, but the certainty of that evidence was rated low. The review could not say how often serious complications or repeat operations occur compared with not operating. Most included studies compared one operation against another, and many were small with weak methods. In practice this means surgery can help people with troublesome bunions, but the honest summary is that the best-quality evidence is limited, and your own symptoms should drive the decision.

sections.heading: What does recovery look like?
sections.body: Recovery depends on the operation and often takes longer than people expect. Some procedures require keeping weight off the foot for two to six weeks, followed by a protective boot for another month or two and physiotherapy. Pain usually settles within about six weeks, but for some people it lasts for months. Ask about your own timeline for work, driving, sitting on the floor and exercise before you decide. Minimally invasive techniques may cause less early swelling and an easier first few weeks, but long-term results appear similar to open surgery, so a smaller scar is not a reason to choose one approach over another.

sections.heading: Will the bunion come back, and is there a right age to operate?
sections.body: Yes, recurrence is possible after any bunion operation. One patient-information source puts it at under 20 percent for the three commonly used approaches, but the true figure varies with the deformity, the technique and the person. In adolescents the bunion has a strong chance of returning if surgery is done before the bones have finished growing, so surgery is usually delayed until growth is nearly complete. A painful bunion in a teenager is still worth assessing, because footwear changes, padding and insoles can help in the meantime.

faqs.a: No. Surgery is considered when a bunion remains painful and limits walking or footwear after non-surgical treatment, or when it causes skin breakdown or pushes the second toe out of position. A bunion that looks prominent but does not bother you does not need an operation.

faqs.q: Can a bunion be corrected without surgery?
faqs.a: No. Wider shoes, padding, toe spacers, orthotics and night splints can reduce pain and may slow progression, but they cannot reverse an established bunion. Products that claim to realign the bone are not backed by solid evidence.

faqs.q: How long does recovery take after bunion surgery?
faqs.a: It varies with the procedure. Some require keeping weight off the foot for two to six weeks, then a boot for another month or two, with physiotherapy. Pain usually settles within about six weeks, though for some people it lasts for months.

faqs.q: Can a bunion come back after surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, it can. One patient-information source reports recurrence below 20 percent for the three common approaches, but the risk depends on the deformity, the technique and the individual. Surgery before the bones have finished growing carries a high chance of recurrence.

faqs.q: Is bunion surgery done only for how the foot looks?
faqs.a: It should not be. Major patient-information sources frame surgery around pain, difficulty walking or wearing shoes, ulceration and toe dislocation, not appearance alone.
